ifstream: The **input file stream** class from `<fstream>`: opens a file for reading, like `cin` pointed at a file. Opening fails (`is_open()` false) if the file does not exist. Its position members are `tellg()`/`seekg()`. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ofstream: The **output file stream** class from `<fstream>`: opens a file for writing, like `cout` pointed at a file. Creates the file if it is missing and, with no mode flags, **truncates** (empties) an existing one. Its position members are `tellp()`/`seekp()`. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
fstream: The file stream class that can both read and write the same file (default mode `in | out`); it has both the g and the p position members. Also the name of the header `<fstream>` that defines all three file stream classes. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
is_open|is_open(): Member function that reports whether a file stream opened successfully; the slides test `if (!f.is_open())` or the shorter `if (!f)` and then print to `cerr` and `exit(1)`. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
cerr: The predefined **error output stream**: a `cout` reserved for error messages (typically shown in red by the IDE). See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
exit|exit(1): Library function (`<cstdlib>`) that terminates the program immediately with the given exit code; a non-zero code such as 1 signals an error. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
close|close(): Member function that closes a file stream and releases the file (`fin.close();`). The stream's destructor also closes it automatically when the object goes out of scope. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
buffer|filebuf|streambuf|stringbuf: Every stream keeps its data in an internal **buffer**: file streams use a `filebuf`, `cin`/`cout`/`cerr` a `streambuf`, and string streams a `stringbuf`. You rarely manage it directly, but `rdbuf()` exposes it. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
rdbuf|rdbuf(): Returns a stream's internal buffer; inserting it into another stream copies everything in one statement: `outFile << inFile.rdbuf();`. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
openmode|ios_base::openmode|open mode: The type of the flags that say how a file is opened: `ios_base::in`, `out`, `app`, `trunc`, `ate`, `binary`, combined with bitwise OR (`ios_base::out | ios_base::app`). See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ios_base::in|in: Open mode flag: allow input operations on the stream (the default for `ifstream`). See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ios_base::out|out: Open mode flag: allow output operations on the stream (the default for `ofstream`); on its own it truncates the file. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ios_base::app|ios::app|app|append: Open mode flag (**app**end): set the stream's position indicator to the end **before each output operation**, so writes always go to the end and nothing is overwritten. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ios_base::trunc|trunc|truncate: Open mode flag: discard the contents of the file when opening. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ios_base::ate|ate: Open mode flag (**at e**nd): set the position indicator to the end of the stream **on opening**, once; later seeks work normally (unlike `app`). See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
ios_base::binary|binary: Open mode flag: open in binary mode, for files that contain binary data rather than text. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
get|get()|put|put(): Character-at-a-time IO: `in.get()` extracts one character (whitespace included) and returns `EOF` at the end of the file; `out.put(c)` writes one character. The slide loop is `while ((c = in.get()) != EOF)`. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
EOF: The value `get()` returns when there is nothing left to read (end of file). Comparing against it ends the character-by-character copy loop. See [File streams](#/comp3522-w2/file-streams).
tellg|tellg()|tellp|tellp(): Return the position of the current character as a `streampos`: **tellg** ("tell get") for input streams, **tellp** ("tell put") for output streams. A fresh `ifstream` reports 0; an `ofstream` opened with `ios::app` on `Hello World` reports 11. See [Seeking](#/comp3522-w2/seeking).
seekg|seekg()|seekp|seekp(): Set the position of the cursor: **seekg** for input streams, **seekp** for output streams (either for `fstream`). Two forms: `seekp(streampos)` absolute, and `seekp(streamoff, seekdir)` relative to `ios::beg`, `ios::cur` or `ios::end`. On `Hello World`: `seekp(6)` gives 6, `seekp(4, ios::beg)` 4, `seekp(-4, ios::end)` 7, then `seekp(-6, ios::cur)` 1. See [Seeking](#/comp3522-w2/seeking).
streampos: The type that stores a position in a stream (what `tellg`/`tellp` return and what the absolute `seekg`/`seekp` take). It is a number, so `end - begin` gives a file's size in bytes. See [Seeking](#/comp3522-w2/seeking).
streamoff: The type that stores an **offset** (a signed distance) used with a `seekdir` in the relative form of `seekg`/`seekp`. See [Seeking](#/comp3522-w2/seeking).
seekdir|ios_base::seekdir: The direction argument of a relative seek: `ios::beg` (from the beginning), `ios::cur` (from the current position) or `ios::end` (from the end), public members of `ios_base`, like C's `SEEK_SET`, `SEEK_CUR`, `SEEK_END`. See [Seeking](#/comp3522-w2/seeking).
ios::beg|ios::cur|ios::end|beg|cur|end: The three seek directions: measure the offset from the **beg**inning, from the **cur**rent position, or from the **end** of the stream. See [Seeking](#/comp3522-w2/seeking).
srand|srand()|seed: Seeds (initializes) C's random number generator; call it **once**, usually with the current time: `srand(time(NULL));`. Re-seeding in a loop replays the same sequence. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
rand|rand()|RAND_MAX: `rand()` (from `<cstdlib>`) returns a pseudo-random integer from 0 to `RAND_MAX`. Fold it into a range with `%`: `rand() % 100` is 0 … 99, `rand() % 100 + 1` is 1 … 100, `rand() % 25 + 2000` is 2000 … 2024; `rand() / (double) RAND_MAX` gives 0.0 … 1.0. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
time|time(NULL)|time(0): Returns the current clock time (`<ctime>`), the usual seed for a random number generator so each run differs. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
random_device: A `<random>` random number generator used in the slides only to produce a random **seed**: `random_device rd; mt19937 generator(rd());`. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
mt19937|default_random_engine|engine: Random number **engines** from `<random>`: `default_random_engine generator(time(0));` or `mt19937 generator(rd());`. An engine produces raw numbers; a distribution shapes them into a range. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
uniform_int_distribution|uniform_real_di: `<random>` distributions that turn an engine's output into evenly spread values in a range: `uniform_int_distribution<> d(a, b)` for ints in a … b inclusive, `uniform_real_distribution<double> d(a, b)` for doubles. Get a value with `d(generator)`. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
array|C-style array|decay: A fixed-size sequence declared as `type name[size]`: `float values[3]`, `char * names[32]` (32 pointers to char), `int scores[] = {1,2,3,4}`; missing initializers are zero-filled. Passed to a function, an array **decays to a pointer** to its first element (`sizeof` drops from 16 to 8 for four ints), so the function works on the original array. See [C-style arrays & random numbers](#/comp3522-w2/arrays-random).
pointer|int*|int *: A variable whose value is a **memory address** (nothing else: not an int, not a string). `int* p` is declared with `*`; it gets a value from `nullptr`, another pointer, `&x`, or `new`. Assigning to the pointer changes where it points; `*p` reaches the box it points at. On the instructor's 64-bit machine every pointer is 8 bytes. See [Pointers, & and *, nullptr](#/comp3522-w2/pointers).
address-of|address of|&x: The `&` operator with **nothing to its left** (`&first`): gives the address of a variable, which is what a pointer stores and what a pointer parameter needs (`swap(&first, &second)`). Not to be confused with `int& x`, a reference declaration. See [Pointers, & and *, nullptr](#/comp3522-w2/pointers).
dereference|*p|dereferencing: Following a pointer to the box it points at with `*`: `*p` reads it, `*p = 5` writes it ("go to where I am pointing and look in the box"). Arrays are dereferenced with `[]`. Dereferencing `nullptr` or a dangling pointer crashes or is undefined behaviour. See [Pointers, & and *, nullptr](#/comp3522-w2/pointers).
nullptr|null pointer: The pointer value meaning "points at nothing". Assign it to every empty pointer so you can test `if (p == nullptr)` instead of holding garbage; never dereference it. See [Pointers, & and *, nullptr](#/comp3522-w2/pointers).
pass by value|call by value: C++'s default: a function parameter receives a **copy** of the argument, so changes inside the function never reach the caller's variable. That is why the plain `swap(int, int)` does nothing to `first` and `second`. See [Pointers, & and *, nullptr](#/comp3522-w2/pointers).
pass by reference|call by reference: Declaring a parameter as a reference (`void swap(int& arg1, int& arg2)`) so the function works on the caller's original variable with no copy; the call looks like a normal call, `swap(first, second)`. Same effect as passing a pointer, but effortless. See [References: the alias](#/comp3522-w2/references).
reference|int&|alias|nickname: A second name for an existing variable, declared with `&` after a type: `int& ref = n;`. It creates no new box, **must** be initialized when created, and can **never** be re-seated; `ref = m` writes m's value into n. References compile to the same assembly as pointers; they exist for programmers. See [References: the alias](#/comp3522-w2/references).
const reference|const int&: A reference that promises not to modify its referent. Unlike a plain reference it may bind to a **temporary** (`const int& r{1}` compiles, `int& r{1}` does not; `const long& ref = n` binds a temporary long copy of the int n). See [References: the alias](#/comp3522-w2/references).
dangling|dangling pointer|dangling refer: A pointer or reference to memory that no longer exists: a deleted heap block (`delete i` leaves i holding the old address) or a local variable after its function returned. Never return a reference or pointer to a local. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
string|std::string|std::string class: C++'s string class (`<string>`, lower-case s): `string s1;` (default constructor), `string s2 = "Hello";`, `string s3{"world!"};`. It knows its own `size()`/`length()`, needs no `\0`, compares with `<`/`==` lexicographically, indexes with `s[0]` or the bounds-checked `s.at(1)`, and gives a C array with `c_str()`. See [std::string & getline](#/comp3522-w2/strings-getline).
c_str|c_str(): Returns the string's characters as a **non-modifiable standard C char array** (null-terminated), for functions that need a C-string. See [std::string & getline](#/comp3522-w2/strings-getline).
at|at()|operator[]: Element access on strings and vectors: `[]` returns a reference with no checking; `at(pos)` checks the bounds and **throws an exception** (`out_of_range`) for a bad index. See [std::vector](#/comp3522-w2/vectors).
getline|getline(): `getline(cin, input)` (from `<string>`) reads a whole line into a string, **tosses the newline**, and returns the stream, so `while (getline(cin, line))` reads until EOF. Stops at EOF (eofbit), at the delimiter (extracted and tossed) or when too many characters were extracted (failbit); with nothing at all to read it sets eofbit **and** failbit and leaves the string unchanged. A third argument sets a custom delimiter. See [std::string & getline](#/comp3522-w2/strings-getline).
istringstream: An input stream over a string (`<sstream>`, really `basic_istringstream<char>`): `istringstream iss{" 123abc"}; iss >> n;` extracts exactly like `cin`, so n is 123 and a following `>> aString` gives `abc`. Reuse one with `iss.clear(); iss.str(line);` or make a fresh one per line. See [istringstream](#/comp3522-w2/stringstream).
str|str()|iss.str: Loads (or returns) the text of a string stream: `iss.str(" 123abc")`. Loading new text does not reset the stream's state bits, hence `iss.clear()` first when reusing. See [istringstream](#/comp3522-w2/stringstream).
clear|clear()|iss.clear: On a stream, resets the state bits (failbit/eofbit) so extraction can continue; on a vector, removes all elements. See [istringstream](#/comp3522-w2/stringstream).
vector|std::vector|vector<int>: The `<vector>` sequence container that grows as you `push_back` (think Java's ArrayList); part of the STL. Members: `push_back`, `size`, `[]`, `at`, `erase(iterator)`, `clear`; iterate with a classic loop or the ranged-for. Capacity doubles when full (1, 2, 4, 8). See [std::vector](#/comp3522-w2/vectors).
push_back|push_back(): Appends a value to the end of a vector, growing it by one element. See [std::vector](#/comp3522-w2/vectors).
erase|erase()|begin(): `v.erase(v.begin()+1)` removes the element at iterator position 1 (the 10 in 5, 10, 15) and shifts the rest down; `begin()` is the iterator to the first element. See [std::vector](#/comp3522-w2/vectors).
ranged-for|range-based for|for-each: C++'s for-each loop: `for (int value : intVector) { ... }` visits every element **by value** (not by index) from first to last. See [std::vector](#/comp3522-w2/vectors).
capacity|capacity(): How many elements a vector's current storage can hold before it must reallocate (g++ doubles it: 1, 2, 4, 8); `size()` is how many elements are actually stored. See [std::vector](#/comp3522-w2/vectors).
new|new[]|new operator: Allocates memory on the heap and **returns a pointer** to it: `int * p = new int{3522};`, `new int` then `*p = 3522`, or `int * arr = new int[5];` for an array. What it creates is a data object that lives until you `delete` it. `new (nothrow)` returns `nullptr` instead of throwing when memory runs out. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
delete|delete[]|delete operator: Frees memory obtained with `new` (`delete p;`) or `new[]` (`delete[] arr;`, the pair must match). It deletes the **object pointed at**, not the pointer, which is left dangling. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
memory leak|leak: Heap memory that can never be freed because nothing points at it any more, e.g. `i = new int{11}; a = new int{99}; i = a;` loses the 11 block. C++ has no garbage collector, so the block stays allocated until the program exits. Fix order: `delete i; i = a; delete i;`. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
heap|stack|dynamic memory|automatic: Automatic (stack) memory (`int i; int a[10];`) is allocated and freed for you when the function returns. Dynamic (heap) memory from `new` exists until you `delete` it, even after the function returns: your responsibility. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
garbage collector|garbage collection: What C++ does **not** have: nothing frees your `new` memory for you, so every `new` needs a matching `delete`. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
nothrow: `new (nothrow) int[n]` (header `<new>`) makes `new` return `nullptr` on failure instead of throwing an exception, so you can check the pointer before using it. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
malloc|calloc|realloc|free: C's four dynamic-memory functions from `stdlib.h`: allocate bytes, allocate zeroed array space, resize, deallocate. C++ replaces them with `new`/`new[]` and `delete`/`delete[]`. See [new, delete and memory leaks](#/comp3522-w2/new-delete).
